90% of AI PM resumes get rejected for the exact same reason: they are filled with prompt engineering buzzwords instead of production architecture. ❌
I have reviewed over 400 AI PM resumes across seed-stage startups and enterprise tech companies.
Most resumes say:
"Prompt engineered GPT-4 workflows to improve customer support."
"Led enterprise Generative AI roadmap and strategy."
To a Head of AI or VP of Product, that signals one thing: you played in the OpenAI playground, but you have never shipped a non-deterministic system to paying users.
If you want callbacks from top AI teams in 2026, every bullet on your resume must pass the C-A-V-R Formula:
Context: What was the real business problem and user scale?
Architecture: What system pattern did you deploy (RAG, cascading, caching, SLMs)?
Verification: How did you measure accuracy and prevent regressions?
ROI: What was the hard impact on cost, latency, and margins?
Here is how top AI PMs rewrite their resume bullets: 👇
1️⃣ Evals & Quality Gates
❌ Pass: "Built internal customer support assistant using Claude and prompt engineering."
✅ Hired: "Spearheaded knowledge copilot across 140,000 monthly queries: established 150-sample Golden Dataset with DeepEval, raising precision from 68% to 94.2% and cutting escalations by 41%."
2️⃣ Latency & Performance
❌ Pass: "Optimized AI response speed and reduced user drop-off in search interface."
✅ Hired: "Architected streaming search pipeline: lowered TTFT from 3.8s to 580ms via SSE streaming and prompt prefix caching, increasing task completion by 28% across 50,000 active users."
3️⃣ Unit Economics & Margin Defense
❌ Pass: "Managed OpenAI API spend and reduced overall model inference costs."
✅ Hired: "Restructured AI stack: introduced 8B SLM cascading and semantic caching, deflecting 64% of volume from GPT-4o and slashing cost-per-query by 72% ($0.042 to $0.012) while defending 99% gross margin."
4️⃣ Autonomous Agents & Tool-Calling
❌ Pass: "Explored autonomous agents and AutoGPT for CRM data entry workflows."
✅ Hired: "Designed multi-agent CRM orchestrator: built strict JSON schema contracts and retry backoffs across Salesforce APIs, reaching 99.4% task reliability across 12,000 weekly workflows."
Stop listing 20 model names.
Stop calling yourself a "prompt engineer."
Show hiring managers that you know how to build golden datasets, manage token budgets, and engineer defensive architecture. 🚀
What is the biggest challenge you face when describing your AI work on your resume? Drop it below! 💬

🇩🇪 Germany will not sponsor you. ❌

This myth is costing AI professionals job opportunities.

September is already underway, and this kicks off a short series for AI professionals considering Europe.

One misconception I still hear constantly: German employers must "sponsor" your visa before they can hire you.

That's not how it works in most cases.

With a qualifying job offer, you apply for your own work permit or EU Blue Card. The employer provides the contract and supporting documents; the residence permit itself comes from immigration authorities — not the company.

Companies across Germany continue hiring AI professionals with experience in:

LLMs and Generative AI
Machine Learning
MLOps
Python
Data Engineering
Cloud platforms
AI-powered product development

Technical skills get your profile noticed. The interview goes deeper.

Can you clearly explain:

Which business problem you solved?
Why that technical approach?
How you evaluated results?
What business impact it created?

If AI opportunities in Germany are on your radar this September, feel free to reach out.

The most persistent blind spot I see in DevOps is the assumption that AI is here to replace the human in the loop. In 2026, the reality is the opposite: AI is becoming the human in the loop, and the DevOps engineer's job is to design the boundaries that AI operates within.

The non-obvious shift is that AI is no longer just a tool for generating code or summarizing logs. It has become an active participant in the delivery decision loop. The latest industry data confirms that pipelines in 2026 are not just CI/CD scripts. They are enforceable delivery contracts where an AI model evaluates every commit against historical failure patterns, cost implications, and compliance rules before deciding whether to promote or rollback. The winning teams are not the ones writing the most YAML. They are the ones designing the guardrails that tell the AI when to act autonomously and when to escalate to a human.

Another blind spot that most teams miss is that AI in DevOps is forcing a fundamental rethinking of how we measure delivery. The shift is from velocity metrics like deployment frequency to outcome metrics like "did this change reduce customer friction" or "did this deployment stay within the cost budget." The teams that are winning are the ones that have embedded AI to correlate deployment events with business outcomes in real time, so they can answer the question "did this release actually move the needle" within minutes, not weeks.

For hiring managers and recruiting leaders: I do not just set up CI/CD pipelines or manage Kubernetes clusters. I design DevOps architectures where AI is a first-class decision maker, not a bolt-on tool. I understand that AI for DevOps is not a feature you add. It is a discipline that requires designing the decision contract, the cost governance model, and the feedback loop that tells the AI when its prediction was wrong. If your team is struggling with AI-generated code quality, autonomous pipelines that cannot distinguish between a routine deployment and a risky one, or a DevOps model that cannot answer "did this release meet its business outcome," I can architect the solution.

The hardest question nobody is asking: When an AI model decides to promote a deployment to production at 3AM based on historical failure patterns, but that deployment introduces a subtle data integrity issue that only appears 72 hours later, who is accountable for that decision, and how do you audit the tradeoff between automation speed and data quality risk?

Lower ceiling (PKR 40K–310K) but the fastest realistic entry point with **zero prior experience needed** — matches what your Jobvior infographic showed (content writing, VA, social media management, graphic design all in the PKR 20K–70K starter range). E-commerce VA work (Shopify/Amazon FBA) and social media VA command the higher end of this bracket.

- Upwork — best for long-term contracts, big client base, but very competitive (10% fee)
- Toptal — no fees, high pay, but hard entry (vetting process)

Here's something I think we get wrong about transformation teams.
We build them as though the project won't change.
But the people you need to define a transformation aren't necessarily the people you need to implement it.
And the people you need during implementation may be completely different from those required for adoption, training and business-as-usual.
Take an AI transformation.

💡 Strategy and governance

Do you really need every one of those capabilities permanently from day one?
Probably not.
A better model is often a strong permanent core, supported by specialist capability that can expand, contract and change as the programme moves forward.
The key question becomes:
Which capability do we need to own, and which do we simply need to access?
That's what I explore in article four of my Beyond Permanent Hiring: The New Workforce Model series.

91% of home sellers used a real estate agent. Why?
At a time when homeowners have access to more real estate information and technology than ever before — online valuations, AI, digital contracts, listing platforms, social media and virtual showing tools — you might expect the role of the real estate agent to be shrinking.
The latest NAR data suggests otherwise.
91% of sellers used an agent, while only 5% sold FSBO — the lowest share on record.
The reason is worth paying attention to.
Sellers aren't simply hiring an agent to put a property online. They are looking for professional guidance on the parts of a transaction that require strategy, judgment and execution.
The top things sellers want from their agents include:
• Marketing the property to potential buyers
• Pricing the home competitively
• Selling within a specific timeframe
• Managing the many details and complexities of the transaction
In fact, 86% of sellers said their agent provided a broad range of services and managed most aspects of the sale.
For me, this reinforces an important point about our industry:
The value of a real estate professional isn't just access to information — it's knowing how to interpret it, build a strategy around it and execute that strategy effectively.
Market conditions change. Buyer behavior changes. Technology changes.
But sellers still need someone who can look at their specific property and situation, determine the right strategy, anticipate challenges, negotiate on their behalf and help get the transaction across the finish line.
That's the part of real estate that technology can't simply replace.

The conversation around AWS in 2026 is still obsessed with compute and database performance, but the most transformative shift I am observing in production environments is how teams are using the new "policy-as-code" integration in AWS Organizations to enforce what I call "zero-trust deployment pipelines."

I have been auditing AWS accounts that adopted the new fine-grained control policies for resource creation and modification. The obvious benefit is that you can block non-compliant infrastructure before it is provisioned. The non-obvious win is that this forces teams to formally define what constitutes a compliant resource before they ever write a Terraform module or CloudFormation template. I have seen teams reduce their security incident rate by 80% simply because the policy enforcement happens at the API layer, not the review layer. The policy becomes the contract, not the pull request.

The second quiet revolution is the maturation of Amazon Bedrock Managed Flows, announced at re:Invent 2026. The overlooked insight is not the ability to chain multiple models together. It is the fact that every flow now has a built-in cost budget and latency budget enforced at the orchestration layer. Teams that adopt this pattern are replacing ad-hoc agent implementations with governed flows that cannot exceed their allocated resources. The most expensive category of AI incidents -- the runaway agent that burns through your monthly inference budget in an hour -- is eliminated by construction.

The most under-discussed capability in the latest AWS Summit announcements is the integration of the new Kiro for iOS with AWS DevOps Agent. The obvious story is mobile access to DevOps workflows. The non-obvious story is what happens to your incident response when a developer can assess code changes and approve releases from their phone during an on-call rotation. Teams adopting this pattern are reducing their mean time to resolve for non-critical incidents by 45% because the approval bottleneck is removed.

For hiring managers: the candidate who can explain why policy-as-code and governed agent flows are not just compliance checkboxes but architectural guarantees for preventing the most expensive security and cost incidents is the one who will design systems that are both auditable and efficient. The candidate who understands that the future of AWS is about enforcement at the platform layer, not detection after deployment, is the one who will protect your cloud from the most common failure modes.

Got an email from LI about their upcoming Talent Connect event coming up at the end of this month. I like what they wrote about what the focus will be: 

Two days. The world's sharpest talent minds. One shared question: what's next for work.

I may not be an expert on that topic but been on LI since 2007. Been working as a contract recruiter for the past 10+ years. Given my role, been a job seeker 8 times in the past 10 years alone. So yes, I know a thing or two about what it's like to help people find a job and look for one myself. 

As far as LI goes, not much has changed since 2007, other than AI. Hiring is broken, all ATS' suck, recruiters ghosting well qualified applicants, scam job posting and so on and so forth year after year. 

Will AI fix those issues, nope. 

I've posted on here before that sooner or later AI will be conducting all initial interviews and people will still make the hiring decision. I look forward to that. 

However, that will not mean that every well qualified applicant will get an interview with a human. You will likely get an interview with an AI Recruiter but that may be about it. 

If there is a job posting for only one opening and over a hundred well qualified applicants apply to it, not every applicant will get to the hiring manager interview stage. A hiring manager is not going to interview 100 people to fill one opening that they need filled asap. They have teams to run and KPI's to hit. 

If I had to pick one pain point that every job seeker has had for the past 15 years or so, it would be applying to jobs and never hearing back even if they are well qualified for the position they applied to. 

How do we try to alleviate that pain point? AI Recruiter initial interviews will go a long way with helping job seekers at least feel a little better that they at least got an interview even if it was with AI. Recruiters will likely conduct an additional interview with those who do well on the AI interviews but not every AI interviewed applicant will get to that stage. You can't expect a recruiter to do additional interviews with 100 people on one job opening that needs to be filled immediately if they are working on 20 or more other positions. 

AI Recruiter interviews may not be an end all solution but it's a start. We have to start somewhere. Then there's the cost issue of using AI to conduct interviews. Pretty sure AI companies are not going to give away that service for free. 

This post is already way too long, I need to get back to work. Time to get back to sending out InMails to potential candidates and have 90% of my messages ignored. Just makes me think about every time I've been in job seeker mode. Last thing I would do is ignore a message from a recruiter about a job opening that may or may not be a good fit. It may be a legit recruiter or it may be a scam. That's a topic for a different post.
